rw: In cultures that value the card as an extension of the person, reading it with respect shows courtesy and regard for the giver before storing it carefully.

ww.Ignore it and put it away without a glan: Putting the card away with no glance signals that you do not value the person or the introduction, which is rude and can damage the new business relationship.
ww.Write on it in front of the giver right: Writing on a card in front of the giver is seen as disrespectful in many cultures because it defaces something treated as a personal representation of them.
ww.Throw it away at once without reading it: Throwing the card away unread is a clear insult, since it dismisses the giver and their details and would end the relationship before it has started.

rw: A strategic alliance is a cooperative partnership where companies pursue shared goals yet remain legally independent, which is exactly what separates it from a merger or takeover.

ww.A bankruptcy in which a firm cannot pay: A bankruptcy is a legal state of insolvency in which a firm cannot pay its debts, which has nothing to do with two firms partnering toward shared goals.
ww.A merger of two companies into one new f: A merger combines two companies into one new firm, so the original companies lose independence, whereas an alliance keeps both firms separate and in control of themselves.
ww.A takeover in which one firm buys anothe: A takeover means one firm buys another and absorbs its assets, which ends the target's independence, while an alliance involves cooperation between firms that stay independent.

rw: A joint venture is formed when two or more parties create a new, separate entity to pursue a specific project, sharing the resources, risks and rewards of it.

ww.A loan from a bank that is repaid with i: A bank loan is borrowed money repaid with interest over time, which is a financing tool and does not create a new jointly owned entity for a project.
ww.A business owned and run by a single per: A business owned and run by one person with no partners is a sole proprietorship, so it cannot be a joint venture, which needs two or more parties.
ww.A sale of company stock to the public th: Selling company stock to the public through an exchange listing is an initial public offering, which raises capital and is unrelated to partners forming a new project entity.

rw: In a franchise, the franchisee pays fees to run a business under the franchisor's established brand and operating system, which is the defining feature of this relationship.

ww.A union deal in which workers agree to t: A union deal is a collective bargaining agreement between workers and an employer on pay and conditions, which has nothing to do with licensing a brand and system.
ww.A loan in which a bank lends money to op: A bank lending money to open a store is a business loan, which is only a financing arrangement and does not involve operating under another firm's brand.
ww.A merger in which two companies combine: A merger combines two companies into one firm, whereas a franchise keeps the two parties separate, with the franchisee running its own outlet under the franchisor's brand.

rw: Eustress is positive stress, such as the excitement before a challenge or a deadline, that motivates and energizes a person, which is what the prefix eu means.

ww.Chronic stress that builds over a long t: Stress that builds up over a long period is chronic stress, which wears people down and is not the energizing, short-term positive kind that eustress describes.
ww.No stress at all, only a state of total: Eustress is still stress, only the helpful kind, so calling it no stress at all and total calm misreads the term; it involves a real but beneficial arousal.
ww.Harmful stress that causes illness and s: Harmful stress that causes illness and strain is distress, the opposite of eustress, so describing it this way confuses the two types of stress.

rw: Distress is negative stress that overwhelms a person's ability to cope and harms health, mood and performance, which sets it apart from the helpful eustress.

ww.Excitement about a new challenge that gi: Excitement about a new challenge that gives energy is eustress, the positive type, so it is the opposite of distress, which drains and harms a person.
ww.Motivating stress that helps a person fo: Motivating stress that helps a person focus is again eustress, the helpful kind, whereas distress is the negative form that reduces performance and wellbeing.
ww.No stress at all, and a state of full re: Distress is real stress, not its absence; a state of full rest and no stress describes relaxation, which is nothing like the strain distress involves.

rw: The Eisenhower matrix sorts tasks into four boxes by urgency and importance, helping a person decide what to do, schedule, delegate or drop, so it is a prioritizing tool.

ww.An org chart that shows who reports to w: An org chart shows reporting lines between people in a company, which is a structure diagram and not a way to sort tasks by urgency and importance.
ww.A budget tool used to plan the income an: A budget tool plans income and costs, which is a financial planning device; the Eisenhower matrix deals with task priority and has no financial figures in it.
ww.A sales chart that shows how many items: A sales chart showing items sold by each store reports results, while the Eisenhower matrix is a planning aid that ranks tasks and does not track sales.

rw: Important but not urgent tasks, such as planning and relationship building, belong in the schedule box, so you set aside time for them before they become urgent.

ww.Delegated: Delegation fits tasks that are urgent but not important, since someone else can handle them; important but not urgent tasks need your own planned time instead.
ww.Done at once: Doing tasks at once is for the urgent and important box; important but not urgent work has no deadline pressure, so it can be planned rather than rushed.
ww.Eliminated: Eliminating applies to tasks that are neither urgent nor important; important tasks have real value, so removing them would waste work that supports long-term goals.

rw: Listening calmly and acknowledging the concern lets the customer feel heard, which lowers their anger and lets you understand the real problem before offering any fix.

ww.Argue back and defend the firm's positio: Arguing back and defending the firm's position escalates the conflict and makes the customer feel unheard, so it does not calm the situation at the start.
ww.Hang up the phone on them right away, qu: Hanging up on an angry customer ends the call without solving anything, damages the firm's reputation and is unprofessional, so it cannot be a good first response.
ww.Ignore them and continue with other task: Ignoring the customer and carrying on with other tasks shows disrespect, leaves the complaint unsolved and will likely make the customer angrier and more likely to leave.

rw: After listening, apologizing for the inconvenience and offering to fix the billing error shows empathy and moves toward a solution, which helps calm the customer and keep their loyalty.

ww.Transfer them without explanation to som: Transferring the customer with no explanation passes the problem along and makes them repeat the story, which adds frustration instead of resolving the billing error.
ww.Tell them to calm down and speak more qu: Telling an upset customer to calm down tends to sound dismissive and often raises their anger, so it does not help once you have listened to the problem.
ww.Blame the customer for the error on thei: Blaming the customer for a billing error is hostile, may be untrue, and risks losing the account, so it fails to solve the problem or keep the customer.

rw: Conflict is a disagreement between people whose needs, goals or ideas differ, which is why it can occur in any team or workplace and has to be managed.

ww.A schedule that lists the dates when eac: A schedule listing the dates when workers take breaks is a rota or timetable for work time, which has nothing to do with people disagreeing over needs or ideas.
ww.Agreement among team members who share t: Agreement among team members who share needs and ideas is harmony or consensus, the opposite of conflict, which arises when needs or ideas differ.
ww.A friendship in which two people spend m: A friendship between two people who spend time together is a social bond, not a conflict, since conflict means disagreement and not companionship.

rw: The accommodating style means giving in to the other party's wishes to keep the peace or the relationship, even when it costs you your own preferences.

ww.Competing to win at all costs in a clash: Competing to win at all costs is the competing or forcing style, which pursues your own goals over the other party's and is the opposite of giving in.
ww.Collaborating to find a joint answer: Collaborating means working with the other party to find a joint answer that satisfies both, which takes effort from both sides and is not simply giving in.
ww.Avoiding the issue and hoping it passes: Avoiding the issue and hoping it passes is the avoiding style, which sidesteps the conflict, whereas accommodating means actively yielding to what the other side wants.

rw: Collaborating means both parties work together to find a solution that satisfies the needs of each, creating a win-win outcome rather than a one-sided result.

ww.Withdrawing from the conflict and avoidi: Withdrawing from the conflict and avoiding the other party is the avoiding style, which leaves the issue unresolved, unlike collaborating, which engages directly to solve it.
ww.Giving in to the other party and droppin: Giving in and dropping your own needs is the accommodating style; collaborating requires that your own needs are met along with those of the other party.
ww.Winning at all costs, even if the other: Winning at all costs while the other party gets nothing is the competing style, which is the opposite of collaborating, where both sides seek an outcome that works.

rw: Compromising means each side gives up something to reach a middle ground, so both get part of what they want, though neither gets everything.

ww.One side wins fully while the other side: One side winning fully while the other loses everything is the competing style, a win-lose result, and compromising instead splits the difference between the two sides.
ww.Both gain fully, with neither side givin: Both sides gaining fully with neither giving anything up is collaborating or a true win-win; compromising always requires each side to surrender part of what it wanted.
ww.Withdrawing from the discussion and leav: Withdrawing from the discussion and leaving the issue open is the avoiding style, which resolves nothing, while compromising reaches a settlement through mutual give and take.

rw: In arbitration a neutral third party hears both sides of the dispute and then makes a decision, which sets it apart from simple negotiation or mediation.

ww.Parties decide alone, with no third part: When the parties decide alone with no third party to help, they are negotiating directly, which differs from arbitration, where an outside neutral party reaches the decision.
ww.A vote held among all the staff to pick: A vote among all staff is a democratic decision method and not arbitration, which relies on a single neutral third party to hear the case and rule.
ww.No decision is reached and the dispute s: Arbitration produces a decision, often binding, so leaving the dispute open with no decision describes avoidance and not a process designed to settle the matter.

rw: A cross-functional team draws members from different departments, such as sales, finance and operations, who combine their skills to work toward a common goal.

ww.A team of interns only, who work in one: A team made only of interns working one summer in a single department is defined by status and time, and says nothing about mixing departments, so it is not cross-functional.
ww.A team from one department who work toge: A team from one department working on tasks within its own unit is a functional team; cross-functional teams, by contrast, cross departmental lines to combine different expertise.
ww.A team of managers only, who meet to rev: A team of managers who review results is a management or leadership team defined by rank, and it does not require members from different functions working on a shared goal.

rw: A virtual team has members in different locations who collaborate through technology such as video calls, email and shared documents, rather than meeting in person.

ww.A team that meets in one room every day: A team that meets in one room every day in the main office is a traditional co-located team, which is the opposite of a virtual team spread across locations.
ww.A game team that plays online against ot: A game team that competes online is a sports or gaming group, and the term virtual team in business refers to remote colleagues working together, not to a game.
ww.A team of robots programmed to complete: A team of robots completing tasks without staff is automation; a virtual team consists of people who work remotely and rely on technology to cooperate.

rw: Team synergy is when the combined effect of the team exceeds the sum of what members could achieve separately, so the whole is greater than its parts.

ww.Competition between members of the team,: Competition between members, who try to beat each other, reduces cooperation and often harms results, whereas synergy comes from working together to achieve more.
ww.Individual work only, in which each pers: Individual work alone and apart from the team produces no combined effect, so it cannot create synergy, which needs members to interact and build on each other's efforts.
ww.Equal tasks given to every member of the: Giving equal tasks to every member is about fairness in workload and says nothing about the added value from cooperation that synergy describes.

rw: Clear individual responsibilities and tracked contributions make each person accountable and visible, which removes the hiding place that social loafing depends on.

ww.Give vague roles so that no one is sure: Vague roles let members hide and make it unclear who is responsible, which encourages social loafing, so giving unclear roles would increase it, not reduce it.
ww.Increase group size so that no single me: Increasing group size lets individuals hide in the crowd and feel less accountable, which makes social loafing worse, as no single member can be singled out.
ww.Ignore effort and treat all members the: Ignoring effort and treating everyone the same gives no reward for working hard and no cost for slacking, which makes slackers more likely to loaf.

rw: A team charter is a written document that defines the team's purpose, roles, norms and goals, giving members a shared agreement on how they will work together.

ww.A pay stub that shows the wages paid to: A pay stub records the wages paid to a worker for a pay period, which is payroll paperwork and not a document that sets up a team's purpose and roles.
ww.A sales report that shows how many units: A sales report showing units sold is a record of results, whereas a charter sets out how the team will operate and what it aims to achieve.
ww.A bus rental contract for transporting t: A bus rental contract for transporting the team is a transport agreement and has nothing to do with defining the team's purpose, roles or norms.

rw: A team facilitator guides the discussion and helps the group work effectively, keeping it on track and making sure everyone can take part, without taking over the decisions.

ww.Doing all the work for the team so that: Doing all the work for the team undermines the group and is not facilitation, which means helping members work well themselves instead of replacing their effort.
ww.Deciding for everyone, so that the group: Deciding for everyone, so the group has no say, is autocratic leadership, whereas a facilitator stays neutral and helps the group reach its own decisions.
ww.Ignoring the team and the discussion unt: Ignoring the team and the discussion until the meeting ends is neglect, and it is the opposite of facilitating, which requires active guidance of the process.

rw: A consensus decision is one that all members can support, even if it is not their first choice, which builds group commitment and a shared agreement.

ww.A random decision reached by chance, suc: A random decision by coin toss or dice involves no discussion or agreement among members, so it cannot be a consensus, which is built on shared support.
ww.A decision by the boss alone, who makes: A decision by the boss alone with no staff input is autocratic, and consensus needs the group to take part and agree to support the outcome.
ww.A majority vote only, in which the large: A majority vote leaves the minority on the losing side without agreement, whereas consensus requires that everyone can accept and support the final decision.

rw: SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound, a set of criteria that makes a goal clear, trackable, realistic and tied to a deadline.

ww.Simple, Minor, Average, Random and Timel: Simple, Minor, Average, Random and Timely are invented words that do not form the SMART acronym; real SMART goals are specific and measurable, not minor or random.
ww.Strong, Mighty, Active, Real and Tough g: Strong, Mighty, Active, Real and Tough is a made-up phrase that sounds forceful, but it is not what the SMART letters stand for in goal setting.
ww.Sudden, Major, Awkward, Rare and Thin go: Sudden, Major, Awkward, Rare and Thin is a nonsense list; none of those words describes a good goal, and they are not the meaning of SMART.

rw: The communication process consists of a sender, a message, a channel, a receiver and feedback, which together describe how information is sent, carried, received and confirmed.

ww.Plan, do and check, then act on the resu: Plan, do and check, then act on the results, is the plan-do-check-act improvement cycle for quality, not the set of elements that make up communication.
ww.Input, output and storage, the parts of: Input, output and storage are the basic parts of a computer system, so they describe how a machine handles data rather than how people communicate.
ww.Buyer, seller and banker, plus a broker: Buyer, seller and banker with a broker or agent are parties in a trade or financial deal, and they are not the elements of the communication process.

rw: Noise is anything that interferes with a message being received accurately, such as background sound, distractions, unclear wording or bias, which distorts the message on its way.

ww.A positive message that raises the mood: A positive message that raises the mood of staff is just a message, and noise means a barrier that distorts communication, so this does not describe noise.
ww.A loud party only, such as one held at t: Noise in communication is broader than a loud party; it includes any interference, physical or mental, so limiting it to a party is far too narrow.
ww.Feedback sent back to the sender to show: Feedback sent back to show understanding is a separate part of the process, and it helps remove errors, whereas noise is what causes the message to be misunderstood.

rw: Feedback is the receiver's response that shows the message was understood, which lets the sender check and correct their communication, completing the communication loop.

ww.The original message sent by the sender: The original message sent by the sender is just the message itself, and feedback is the response that comes back from the receiver afterward.
ww.The channel, or medium, used to carry th: The channel or medium carries the message between people, such as email or speech, and feedback is the reply that returns along that route.
ww.Noise that interferes with the message a: Noise is interference that disrupts a message in transit, which is a barrier, whereas feedback is the receiver's helpful response that confirms understanding.

rw: Crossed arms and no eye contact commonly signal disinterest or defensiveness, since the closed posture and avoided gaze suggest the person is withdrawn or resisting the message.

ww.Full comprehension and agreement: Full comprehension and agreement would usually show through open posture, nodding and eye contact, whereas crossed arms with no eye contact suggest the opposite.
ww.Enthusiasm and strong interest: Enthusiasm and strong interest are normally shown by leaning forward, facing the speaker and keeping eye contact, so crossed arms do not fit that picture.
ww.Strong agreement and trust: Agreement and trust are typically shown by open body language and steady eye contact, so a closed posture without eye contact points away from that.

rw: Paraphrasing is restating what someone said in your own words to confirm understanding, which shows active listening and lets the speaker correct any misunderstanding.

ww.Disagreeing with what someone said and g: Disagreeing and giving your own view is responding or debating, and paraphrasing instead means restating what the speaker said to check you understood them.
ww.Copying word for word what someone said,: Copying word for word is repeating or quoting, while paraphrasing puts the message in your own words, which proves you understood the meaning and not just the sounds.
ww.Ignoring the speaker and thinking about: Ignoring the speaker while thinking about your reply is poor listening, and paraphrasing is the reverse, since it needs close attention to what was said.

rw: A face-to-face or live conversation conveys tone and body language and allows instant questions, which makes it the best channel for complex or sensitive news.

ww.A text sent quickly to many people: A quick text sent to many people lacks tone and room for questions, so it is a poor channel for a message that is complex or sensitive.
ww.A mass email sent to the whole staff: A mass email to the whole staff is impersonal and gives no chance for immediate feedback, which makes it unsuitable for a sensitive and complex message.
ww.A sticky note left on a coworker's desk: A sticky note on a desk is brief and impersonal, and it could be missed or misread, so it cannot carry a complex or sensitive message well.

rw: A short email or message suits a quick, simple reminder because it is fast, cheap and easy to send, and it needs no one's time to meet.

ww.A conference with a panel: A conference with a panel takes heavy planning and many people's time, which is far too much effort for a quick and simple reminder.
ww.A long meeting of all staff: A long meeting of all staff uses a lot of time across the firm for a trivial point, so it is inefficient for a simple reminder.
ww.A formal letter sent by mail: A formal letter sent by mail is slow and costly, so it is poorly suited to a quick reminder that needs to arrive right away.

rw: Tone in writing is the writer's attitude toward the reader and subject, conveyed through word choice, such as friendly, formal or firm wording.

ww.The length of the document in total page: The length of the document in pages is its size, and tone refers to the attitude a writer conveys and not to how long the document is.
ww.The font size used for the text in the m: The font size used for the text is a formatting choice about appearance, whereas tone concerns the writer's attitude shown through the words chosen.
ww.The paper quality of the printed message: The paper quality of a printed message is a physical feature of the page and has no bearing on the attitude that tone describes.

rw: The you attitude means focusing on the reader's needs and benefits, which makes a message more persuasive and respectful because it shows what is in it for them.

ww.Being vague and unclear in what you writ: Being vague and unclear hurts the reader and breaks the principles of clear writing, and the you attitude instead centers on what the reader needs.
ww.Using slang and casual words in every me: Using slang and casual words in every message ignores the audience and context, and it is not what the you attitude means in business writing.
ww.Focusing on yourself and the firm in eac: Focusing on yourself and the firm is the opposite of the you attitude, which shifts the focus onto the reader, their needs and what they gain.

rw: An agenda outlines the topics to be covered and keeps the meeting focused and on schedule, so participants know the purpose and can prepare in advance.

ww.To record the minutes of the last meetin: Recording the minutes of the last meeting is the purpose of the minutes, which are written afterward, while an agenda is prepared beforehand to guide the meeting.
ww.To lengthen meetings and add more topics: An agenda is meant to keep meetings efficient, so lengthening the meeting and adding topics each time works against its purpose of staying focused.
ww.To invite guests only and list the peopl: Inviting guests and listing attendees is an invitation or attendance list, and an agenda mainly lists the topics and order of business, not who attends.

rw: An employee sending a progress report to a manager moves information from a lower level to a higher one, which is the definition of upward communication.

ww.Coworkers chatting together about their: Coworkers chatting about weekend plans is peer-level, informal or horizontal communication, so it does not travel upward toward someone higher in the organization.
ww.A manager giving orders to a team about: A manager giving orders to a team sends information downward from a higher level to a lower one, so it is downward communication and not upward.
ww.A CEO memo to all staff about a new comp: A CEO memo to all staff about policy flows from the top down to employees, so it is an example of downward communication and not upward.

rw: The grapevine is the informal communication network within an organization, where rumors and news spread by word of mouth outside official channels.

ww.An official memo sent out to all staff b: An official memo from the head office is formal communication through a sanctioned channel, which is the opposite of the informal grapevine.
ww.A garden where grapes grow on vines and: A garden where grapes grow is the literal meaning of a vineyard, but in business the grapevine is a figure of speech for informal workplace talk.
ww.The formal chain of command from the man: The formal chain of command from managers to staff is the official communication structure, and the grapevine is the informal network that runs outside of it.

rw: Distributive negotiation divides a fixed resource, so one side's gain is the other side's loss, which is why it is also called win-lose negotiation.

ww.Expanding the pie for both sides, so tha: Expanding the pie so both sides gain more value is integrative negotiation, which seeks win-win results, and it is the opposite of the distributive approach.
ww.Avoiding negotiation by refusing to talk: Avoiding negotiation by refusing to talk is withdrawal, and it is not distributive negotiation, which involves active bargaining over a fixed amount.
ww.Sharing equally always, whatever each si: Sharing equally always, whatever each side has contributed, is a fixed rule of fairness and does not describe distributive bargaining, in which each side pushes for more.

rw: Integrative negotiation looks for solutions that create value for all parties by exploring shared interests, which enlarges the pie and produces win-win results.

ww.Avoiding talks and leaving the matter un: Avoiding talks and leaving the matter unresolved is withdrawal, whereas integrative negotiation actively seeks a result that benefits every party.
ww.Dividing a fixed amount between the side: Dividing a fixed amount fairly between the sides describes distributive negotiation, which treats the pie as limited, unlike the value-creating integrative approach.
ww.Forcing a deal on the other side by usin: Forcing a deal on the other side with threats is coercion and ignores their interests, which is the opposite of the cooperative integrative approach.

rw: An interest is the underlying need or reason behind a demand, while a position is what the party says it wants, so uncovering interests opens more solutions.

ww.They are identical, since an interest an: Interests and positions are not identical; a position is what a party says it wants, while an interest is the underlying need behind that demand.
ww.A position is the underlying need and an: This reverses the terms, since the position is the stated demand and the interest is the underlying need, so calling the position the need is incorrect.
ww.An interest is a price, and a position i: An interest is not a price, and a position is not a cost paid; both terms describe a party's stated demand versus its real needs, not money.

rw: Anchoring means making the first offer to set the starting point of the discussion, which then influences the range in which the final deal is likely to land.

ww.Staying silent for a long time to put pr: Staying silent to pressure the other side is a separate tactic, since anchoring depends on putting a first number on the table, not on silence.
ww.Ending the talks early by leaving the ro: Ending talks early by leaving the room with no offer made is a walkout, and anchoring requires an actual first offer that frames the bargaining.
ww.Walking away from the table to show that: Walking away to show a lack of interest is a bluff or a walk-away tactic, whereas anchoring sets the starting point by being the first to name terms.

rw: A concession is giving up something, such as price or terms, to move toward agreement, and it signals willingness to cooperate and keeps negotiation moving.

ww.Making a threat to the other side to get: Making a threat to get your way is coercion and gives nothing up, while a concession is a voluntary give that helps move both sides closer to a deal.
ww.Winning everything, giving the other sid: Winning everything and giving the other side nothing is the opposite of a concession, which by definition involves yielding some point to the other party.
ww.Walking away from the table with no deal: Walking away from the table with no deal is a breakdown of talks; a concession is a step made in order to reach a deal, not to leave without one.

rw: A Gantt chart is a bar chart showing a project schedule, with each task as a bar along a timeline, so you can see start dates, durations and overlaps.

ww.A pie chart that shows the shares of a w: A pie chart shows shares of a whole as slices of a circle, which suits proportions and not the scheduling of tasks along a timeline.
ww.A balance sheet that lists the assets an: A balance sheet lists a firm's assets and debts at one date, which is a financial statement and not a tool that displays project tasks over time.
ww.An org chart that shows who reports to w: An org chart shows who reports to whom within a company, which is a structure diagram, whereas a Gantt chart displays a timetable of project tasks.

rw: The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent tasks, and it sets the minimum project duration, because any delay on it pushes back the finish date.

ww.The shortest task list that a team could: The shortest task list does not determine duration; the critical path is about the longest chain of dependent tasks, not the fewest tasks.
ww.A list of risks that a team might face,: A ranked list of risks by likelihood is a risk register or risk matrix, which is a separate tool and does not set the minimum project duration.
ww.A budget path that shows how money flows: A budget path showing how money flows is a funding or cash flow view, and the critical path concerns task dependencies and timing, not money.

rw: A milestone is a significant checkpoint or achievement in the schedule, such as finishing a phase or approval, which marks progress toward the project's completion.

ww.A budget item that lists the cost of a s: A budget item listing the cost of a single task is a cost line, whereas a milestone marks a point in the schedule and carries no cost by itself.
ww.A stone marker set beside a road to show: A stone marker beside a road is the literal meaning of the word, but in project management a milestone is a schedule checkpoint, not a roadside object.
ww.A task owner in charge of finishing one: A task owner in charge of finishing one job is a responsible person or assignee, and a milestone is an event in the plan, not a person.

rw: Scope creep is the uncontrolled expansion of a project's requirements after it has started, which typically leads to delays, cost overruns and missed deadlines.

ww.Finishing early because the project need: Finishing early because the project needs fewer tasks is a schedule gain or a descoping, and scope creep is the opposite, where more and more work gets added.
ww.Cutting scope to remove tasks that are n: Cutting scope to remove tasks not in the plan is a controlled reduction of scope, while scope creep is growth that happens without any approved change.
ww.Reducing cost by finding cheaper supplie: Reducing cost by finding cheaper suppliers is a cost saving measure and does not involve changes in requirements, so it is unrelated to scope creep.

rw: A project stakeholder is anyone with an interest in the project or who is affected by it, including sponsors, team members, customers, suppliers and the community.

ww.Only investors who have put money into t: Investors who put money in are stakeholders, but not the only ones; the term covers anyone with an interest in or affected by the project, so the word only fails.
ww.Only the manager who leads the project a: The project manager is one stakeholder among many, so restricting the term to that manager leaves out the customers, sponsors, staff and others affected by the project.
ww.Only the team members who do the tasks i: Team members who do the tasks are stakeholders, but not the only ones, so saying only those members misses sponsors, clients and others with an interest.

rw: A WBS divides a project into smaller, manageable tasks and deliverables, which makes it easier to estimate, assign and track work across the whole project.

ww.A budget summary of the costs of the who: A budget summary of costs is a cost estimate, whereas a work breakdown structure divides the project's scope into smaller deliverables and tasks.
ww.A schedule of breaks for staff who work: A schedule of breaks for staff is a rota and has nothing to do with the WBS, which is a planning tool for decomposing project work.
ww.An org chart showing the reporting lines: An org chart showing reporting lines is an organization structure, while the WBS breaks down the work to be done and not the people who do it.

rw: Agile is an iterative approach that delivers work in short cycles with frequent feedback, which lets the team adapt to change and improve with each round.

ww.A rigid single-phase plan that is fixed: A rigid single-phase plan fixed at the start and never changed describes a traditional waterfall style, which is the opposite of the adaptive agile approach.
ww.A method with no planning, where the tea: Agile still involves planning for each short cycle, so a method with no planning that just starts work is a misreading of the approach.
ww.A budgeting tool used to plan the costs: A budgeting tool for costs and income over several years is a financial plan, and agile is a way of managing and delivering project work.

rw: A sprint in Scrum is a short, fixed period, often one to four weeks, in which the team completes a set amount of work and delivers an increment.

ww.A budget set aside by a firm to pay for: A budget set aside to pay running costs is a financial allocation, while a sprint is a time period in Scrum in which a team completes set work.
ww.A race run over a short distance in whic: A short race in which athletes run fast is the sports meaning of sprint, but in Scrum the word refers to a fixed work period, not a race.
ww.A meeting about bonuses, held each quart: A meeting about bonuses each quarter is a pay review, and a sprint is a development cycle, so it has nothing to do with deciding extra pay.

rw: Theory X holds that employees dislike work, avoid responsibility and need close supervision and control, so managers using it direct and monitor staff closely.

ww.The view that no one works unless they a: Theory X does not rest on large rewards; it assumes people dislike work and need supervision and control, and not that rewards alone move them, so this describes a different view.
ww.The view that employees enjoy work and s: Enjoying work and seeking responsibility on their own is Theory Y, the opposite view, in which employees are self-motivated and need little control.
ww.The view that pay is irrelevant to emplo: Theory X does not claim that pay is irrelevant; it assumes people work for pay and under control, so saying pay is irrelevant to staff misstates it.

rw: Theory Y holds that employees are self-motivated, enjoy work and seek responsibility, so managers using it give autonomy and trust instead of tight control.

ww.The view that employees dislike work and: Believing that employees dislike work and need close supervision is Theory X, the opposite assumption, and not the positive view held in Theory Y.
ww.The view that employees need strict cont: Needing strict control and threats to work is also a Theory X assumption, since Theory Y says people can direct themselves without such pressure.
ww.The view that pay is everything to worke: Theory Y does not say pay is everything; it says people are motivated by many things including responsibility and growth, so a pay-only view is wrong.

rw: The Hawthorne studies found that attention and social factors can improve worker productivity, since workers produced more when they felt observed and valued by researchers.

ww.Only pay matters to workers, and nothing: The Hawthorne studies found that social factors and attention affected output, so saying only pay matters and nothing else does contradicts the findings.
ww.Breaks reduce output, since workers who: The studies did not find that rest breaks reduce output; instead they showed that attention and social factors, not breaks alone, raised productivity in many cases.
ww.Lighting always lowers output as workers: Lighting was tested, but output rose even when the lighting changed in various ways, so the claim that bright light always lowers output is not what was found.

rw: Scientific management is Frederick Taylor's approach of studying tasks to find the most efficient methods, then training workers to follow them to raise productivity.

ww.Managing by intuition and gut feeling, w: Managing by intuition and gut feeling with no studies or data is the reverse of scientific management, which relies on careful study and measurement of work.
ww.Managing a laboratory, where scientists: Managing a laboratory is a literal use of the word science and not the management theory, which concerns the study of tasks to improve efficiency in factories.
ww.Managing with no data, using only the ru: Managing with only rules of thumb is the old way that Taylor sought to replace; scientific management uses data and time studies instead of loose habits.

rw: Henri Fayol contributed principles and functions of management, such as planning, organizing, commanding, coordinating and controlling, which still shape management teaching today.

ww.Scientific time studies of each task, us: Scientific time studies of each task came from Frederick Taylor, who founded scientific management, whereas Fayol is known for general management principles.
ww.Assembly line design, where a product mo: Assembly line design was associated with Henry Ford and mass production, and it was not Fayol's work, which focused on administrative principles and management functions.
ww.The Hawthorne studies of worker output,: The Hawthorne studies were carried out at the Western Electric plant by researchers such as Elton Mayo, not by Henri Fayol, who wrote on administration.

rw: Management by walking around means managers circulate to interact informally with employees and observe the work, which builds rapport and reveals problems early.

ww.A fitness plan in which staff walk aroun: Management by walking around is not a fitness plan; it describes managers moving through the workplace to talk with staff, and it has nothing to do with exercise.
ww.Managing from a locked office, with litt: Managing from a locked office with little contact is the reverse of walking around, which depends on frequent, visible, informal contact with employees.
ww.Remote management only, in which a manag: Remote management from home without site visits is the opposite of walking around, which requires the manager to be physically present among the staff.

rw: After the problem is defined, the next step is to identify alternatives, meaning the possible courses of action, so that the best one can be chosen.

ww.Evaluate the outcome: Evaluating the outcome comes at the end of the decision process, after the choice has been made and carried out, and not right after defining the problem.
ww.Implement the decision: Implementing the decision happens after alternatives are listed and one is chosen, so it cannot come directly after the problem is defined.
ww.Celebrate the result: Celebrating the result is not a step in the decision process, and in any case it would come after the outcome, not right after defining the problem.

rw: A programmed decision is a routine decision handled by established procedures or rules, such as reordering stock, because the situation recurs and the answer is known.

ww.A computer-only decision made without an: Programmed decisions are made by people following set procedures, so calling them computer-only with no human input misreads the term, which is about routine, not machines.
ww.A random decision made by chance with no: A random decision made by chance with no rules is the opposite of programmed, which relies on established rules and set methods.
ww.A unique one-time decision made by a man: A unique one-time decision with no rules is a non-programmed decision, the other category, whereas programmed decisions cover repeated, routine matters.

rw: A non-programmed decision is unique and complex and requires judgment, because the situation is new and no established procedure exists to guide the choice.

ww.A repeated decision made often by set ru: A repeated decision made often by set rules is programmed, the opposite kind, since non-programmed decisions are new and have no ready-made procedure.
ww.A routine decision made by the same set: A routine decision made by the same procedure is also programmed, whereas non-programmed decisions arise in new situations that do not fit set routines.
ww.A decision by computer following set rul: A decision made by computer following set rules is programmed in nature, since the rules decide it; non-programmed decisions need human judgment.

rw: Maslow's hierarchy is a theory that people are motivated by needs, ordered from basic survival up to self-actualization, with higher needs arising once lower ones are met.

ww.A schedule that shows when each employee: A schedule showing when each employee works is a work roster, which is administrative planning and not a theory of what motivates people at work.
ww.A pay scale that sets what workers earn: A pay scale setting what workers earn at each level is a compensation structure, and Maslow's hierarchy is about human needs and motivation, not pay grades.
ww.A list of job duties that tells each emp: A list of job duties is a job description, whereas Maslow's hierarchy is a motivation theory arranged in levels from physiological needs to self-actualization.

rw: Physiological needs, such as food, water and rest, sit at the base of Maslow's hierarchy and must generally be met before higher needs can motivate a person.

ww.Self-actualization: Self-actualization sits at the top of the hierarchy and is pursued only after the lower needs are met, so it cannot be the first need.
ww.Belonging needs: Belonging needs are the third level, after physiological and safety needs, so they generally come into play only once those basic needs are met.
ww.Esteem and status: Esteem and status are the fourth level, which appears only after physiological, safety and belonging needs, so it is not the first need to meet.

rw: Self-actualization means realizing one's full potential, the highest level in Maslow's hierarchy, where a person pursues growth, creativity and personal fulfillment.

ww.Basic needs for food and shelter: Basic needs for food and shelter are physiological needs at the base of the hierarchy, not the top level of self-actualization.
ww.Job security and a pension: Job security and a pension fall under safety needs, the second level, whereas self-actualization is about growth and personal fulfillment at the top.
ww.Friendship and social ties: Friendship and social ties are belonging needs, the third level, and they differ from self-actualization, which is about reaching one's fullest personal potential.

rw: Herzberg's hygiene factors, such as pay and working conditions, prevent dissatisfaction when adequate, but they do not motivate by themselves, since their presence only removes complaints.

ww.Factors unrelated to work that have no e: Hygiene factors are not unrelated to work; they are job context factors that do affect how people feel, since poor ones cause dissatisfaction.
ww.Factors that always motivate workers and: Factors that always motivate and drive above-expected performance are motivators in Herzberg's theory, whereas hygiene factors only prevent dissatisfaction and do not motivate by themselves.
ww.Cleanliness tips only, such as how to ke: Hygiene in Herzberg's theory is a term for job context factors and not cleanliness, so tips on tidiness and handwashing miss its meaning entirely.

rw: Motivators are factors such as achievement and recognition that create satisfaction and drive higher effort, because they relate to the content of the work itself.

ww.Working conditions only, such as the off: Working conditions are hygiene factors, which prevent dissatisfaction, whereas motivators relate to the work itself, such as achievement, recognition and growth.
ww.Salary only, meaning the pay and raises: Salary is a hygiene factor in Herzberg's theory, and it prevents dissatisfaction but does not create lasting satisfaction, so it is not a motivator.
ww.Company policies only, such as the rules: Company policies are hygiene factors that can cause dissatisfaction if poor, while motivators come from the job itself, such as responsibility and advancement.

rw: Expectancy theory says people are motivated when they expect effort to lead to performance, and performance to lead to rewards they value.

ww.People never change their behavior, what: Expectancy theory does say behavior responds to rewards and expectations, so claiming that people never change behavior whatever rewards they are offered contradicts it.
ww.People are random in their actions, and: Expectancy theory offers a rational explanation of why people choose effort levels, so claiming no theory can explain their choices rejects the point of it.
ww.People work only for fear of losing the: Expectancy theory is not about fear of job loss; it concerns beliefs about effort, performance and valued rewards, so a fear-only view misstates the theory.

rw: Equity theory says people compare their inputs and rewards with those of others and seek fairness, and they adjust effort when they feel treated unfairly.

ww.Rewards do not matter to workers, who ca: Equity theory holds that rewards matter a great deal, since workers compare outcomes to others, so claiming rewards do not matter reverses the theory.
ww.Everyone earns equally, whatever the hou: Equity theory is about perceived fairness, not equal pay for everyone, so saying all earn equally whatever hours or results misreads what fairness means.
ww.Only managers matter in the firm, since: Equity theory centers on how employees view fairness in comparison with peers, not on managers alone, so saying only managers matter ignores the workers' view.

rw: Goal-setting theory says specific, challenging goals combined with feedback lead to higher performance than easy or vague goals, because they focus effort and persistence.

ww.No goals are best, since people work har: Goal-setting theory finds that having goals improves performance, so claiming that no goals are best contradicts the research on focus and effort.
ww.Easy goals always best, since they are r: Easy goals do not raise output, because goal-setting theory shows that challenging goals drive higher effort than goals which are reached with little effort.
ww.Vague goals work best, since workers can: Vague goals give workers no clear target, so they perform worse; goal-setting theory shows that specific goals work better than vague ones.

rw: Business ethics is the set of principles guiding right and wrong conduct in business, covering honesty, fairness and responsibility to customers, staff and society.

ww.Tax strategy, the planning of how a firm: Tax strategy is about planning how a firm pays less tax, which is a financial topic and not the principles of right and wrong conduct.
ww.Accounting rules, the standards for how: Accounting rules set standards for recording sales and finances, which is a technical field, whereas ethics concerns moral principles about conduct in business.
ww.Business law only, the statutes that gov: Business law covers statutes such as contract rules, but ethics goes beyond law to moral principles about right and wrong, so saying law only is too narrow.

rw: Something can be legal yet still considered unethical, since laws set minimum rules while ethics reflects moral standards that can be stricter than the law.

ww.They are always identical, so a legal ac: Legal and ethical are not always identical; laws set minimum standards, and some legal acts are still seen as wrong, so a legal act is not always ethical.
ww.Ethical means illegal, and legal means e: Ethical does not mean illegal, and legal does not mean ethical in all cases, because the two ideas overlap but are different standards.
ww.Legal means always right, and no legal a: Legal does not mean always right; some legal actions, such as misleading but lawful marketing, are still judged wrong, so calling every legal act right is false.

rw: Awarding a contract to her brother's firm without disclosure is a conflict of interest, since her personal tie could bias a decision she should make impartially.

ww.Standard open bidding: Standard open bidding means all suppliers compete fairly under the same rules, whereas steering a contract to a relative in secret is the opposite of open bidding.
ww.Legally required by law: No law requires her to give a contract to a relative, and hiding the relationship is the problem, so saying the law requires it is false.
ww.Good practice here: Hiding a family tie while awarding a contract undermines fairness and trust, so it is not good practice; proper practice is to disclose and step aside.

rw: Insider trading is trading securities using confidential information not available to the public, which gives the trader an unfair advantage and is illegal in most countries.

ww.Trading after public news has been relea: Trading after public news is released and widely shared uses information everyone has, which is legal, so it differs from insider trading, which depends on secret information.
ww.Trading in a company's building, on the: Insider trading has nothing to do with where trading occurs, such as a floor of offices; the issue is the use of confidential information, not the location.
ww.Trading with a broker through an account: Trading through a legal broker account open to any member of the public is ordinary legal investing and does not involve secret, nonpublic information.

rw: A bribe is giving something of value to improperly influence a decision, such as paying an official to win a contract, which is illegal and unethical.

ww.A normal gift under company policy, such: A normal gift allowed under company policy, such as a card or flowers, is not meant to sway a decision, so it is not a bribe.
ww.A fair price that a buyer pays for goods: A fair price paid by a buyer in an open market is an ordinary transaction for goods, with no improper influence on anyone's decision.
ww.A thank-you note sent to a client after: A thank-you note sent to a client after a meeting is a courtesy with no value given to sway a decision, so it is not a bribe.

rw: The FCPA is a U.S. law that prohibits bribing foreign officials to win or keep business, and it also requires accurate company records of payments.

ww.A U.S. tax law that sets income tax rate: The FCPA is not a tax law; it addresses bribery of foreign officials, while income tax rates for firms are set by separate tax legislation.
ww.A U.S. law on imports that limits goods: Limits on imported goods come from trade and tariff laws, and the FCPA is an anti-bribery statute, so it does not regulate imports from abroad.
ww.A U.S. hiring law that sets the age to w: Setting the age to work in a firm falls under child labor and employment law, while the FCPA deals with corruption and bribery abroad.

rw: Span of control equals the number of direct reports a manager supervises, and she supervises 8, so her span of control is 8.

ww.1: A span of control of 1 would mean she supervises a single person, but the question says she has 8 direct reports, so it is 8.
ww.16: Sixteen would double the direct reports she actually has; span of control is just the count of people reporting to her, which is 8.
ww.80: Span of control is the number of direct reports, which is 8, so 80 would require multiplying by ten with no basis in the numbers given.

rw: Turnover rate equals employees who left divided by employees at the start, so 10 divided by 50 is 0.20, or 20 percent.

ww.5 percent: Five percent would mean 2.5 people left, but turnover is departures divided by average staff, and 10 divided by 50 is 0.20, not 0.05.
ww.40 percent: Forty percent would apply to 20 of 50 staff leaving; it likely subtracts the leavers wrongly, because 10 divided by 50 equals 20 percent.
ww.10 percent: Ten percent mistakes the count of leavers, 10, for a percentage; the rate is 10 divided by 50 employees, which equals 20 percent.

rw: Variance is actual minus budget, 44,000 minus 40,000, which is 4,000, and dividing by the 40,000 budget gives 10 percent, which is over budget.

ww.4 percent over budget: Four percent over budget uses 4,000 divided by 100,000 or a similar slip; the variance of 4,000 should be divided by the 40,000 budget, which gives 10 percent.
ww.110 percent over budget: One hundred ten percent compares actual cost to budget, since 44,000 divided by 40,000 is 1.10, but the overrun is only the 10 percent above budget.
ww.10 percent under budget: The actual cost of 44,000 is above the 40,000 budget, so the project is over budget, not under budget, and the variance is 10 percent over.

rw: Setting goals and planning is planning, assigning tasks is organizing, motivating is leading, and checking results is controlling, so she used all four functions.

ww.Planning only, as other steps are part o: She did more than plan, since assigning tasks is organizing, motivating staff is leading and checking results is controlling, so planning only is incomplete.
ww.Hiring, firing, paying and training staf: Hiring, firing, paying and training are staffing and human resource tasks, and they do not match the goals, plans, assignments, motivation and checking she carried out.
ww.Marketing, selling, pricing and promotin: Marketing, selling, pricing and promoting are business activities in the marketing mix, not the management functions shown by her goal setting and checking of results.

rw: Reporting that slow computers cause missed orders and asking for a fix is controlling, since she compares performance with expectations and acts to correct the deviation.

ww.Planning: Planning sets goals and decides actions in advance, whereas reporting a problem and requesting a fix is a response to results, which is part of controlling.
ww.Organizing: Organizing means arranging people, tasks and resources, and she is not assigning work here, so reporting a problem and asking for a fix does not match it.
ww.Leading: Leading involves motivating and guiding people, whereas she is reporting a performance problem and seeking a fix, which is corrective action and not motivation.

rw: Deciding who works which shift and does which task is organizing, since she arranges people and resources to carry out the work.

ww.Planning: Planning sets goals and decides what to do ahead of time, but deciding who works which shift and task is arranging resources, which is organizing.
ww.Leading: Leading means motivating and guiding people, and assigning shifts and tasks is arranging work and not inspiring or directing people's effort.
ww.Controlling: Controlling compares results with goals and corrects problems, whereas assigning shifts and tasks sets up the work beforehand, which makes it organizing.

rw: First-line managers supervise daily work, so they rely most on technical skills, meaning job-specific knowledge to guide, train and help their staff.

ww.Conceptual skills: Conceptual skills, the ability to see the big picture, matter most to top managers, and first-line managers use them less often than technical skills.
ww.Legal skills: Legal skills are specialized knowledge rather than a core management skill, and first-line managers use technical skills far more often.
ww.Public relations: Public relations is a function for handling the firm's image, and it is a top-level concern, not the skill first-line managers use most often.

rw: She delegates the task but remains responsible for the result, which shows that responsibility cannot be delegated away entirely, though authority and tasks can be.

ww.Delegation transfers all accountability: Delegation does not transfer all accountability to staff, because the manager remains answerable for the outcome even after assigning the task to someone else.
ww.Delegation removes the need for any foll: Delegation does not remove the need for follow-up, since the manager who keeps ultimate responsibility must still check progress and results.
ww.Delegation is a sign of weak management: Delegation is a sign of strong management when done well, since it develops staff and frees time, so calling it weakness misreads the situation.

rw: With 40 staff and a span of control of 8, she needs 40 divided by 8, which is 5 supervisors.

ww.8: Eight is the target span of control, not the number of supervisors; the number needed is 40 staff divided by 8 per supervisor.
ww.32: Thirty-two comes from subtracting 8 from 40, but supervisors needed equal staff divided by span, which is 40 divided by 8, not 40 minus 8.
ww.320: Three hundred twenty comes from multiplying 40 by 8, but the correct operation is division, since each supervisor handles 8 staff, giving 5.

rw: Launching a new product line in three years is a long-term, company-wide direction, which is a strategic plan covering broad goals over several years.

ww.An operational plan: An operational plan covers day-to-day or short-term activities of a unit, so a three-year company goal is too broad and long-range for it.
ww.A contingency plan: A contingency plan is a backup for events that might go wrong, while a three-year product launch is a primary long-term goal and not a backup.
ww.A tactical plan: A tactical plan translates strategy into medium-term actions for departments, whereas a three-year company-wide launch sets the overall direction, which is strategic.

rw: A weekly schedule of who bakes what and when is a short-term, day-to-day plan for one unit, which makes it an operational plan.

ww.A mission statement: A mission statement describes a firm's purpose and reason for existing, not a weekly schedule of tasks, so it does not fit the example.
ww.A strategic plan: A strategic plan sets long-term direction for the whole firm, and a weekly bakery schedule is short-term and local, so it is operational and not strategic.
ww.A vision statement: A vision statement describes what the firm hopes to become in the future, and a weekly baking schedule is a short-term plan of tasks.

rw: A decision matrix scores each option on several criteria, such as price, quality and delivery, and totals them, so the highest total points to the best choice.

ww.A Gantt chart: A Gantt chart shows project tasks and timelines as bars, so it is a scheduling tool and not a way to score suppliers against several criteria.
ww.A Pareto chart: A Pareto chart ranks causes of problems by frequency to show the vital few, and does not compare options against weighted criteria like supplier scores.
ww.A fishbone diagram: A fishbone diagram maps the causes of a problem, and it is used to find root causes and not to score and rank supplier options.

rw: Tasks listed with start and end dates as bars along a calendar form a Gantt chart, the standard visual tool for project schedules.

ww.An org chart: An org chart shows reporting lines among people and positions, not tasks with start and end dates laid out as bars on a calendar.
ww.A pie chart: A pie chart shows parts of a whole as slices and has no timeline, so it cannot show tasks with start and end dates.
ww.A balance sheet: A balance sheet lists a firm's assets, debts and equity at a given date, which is a financial report and not a task scheduling tool.

rw: Moving decision-making authority from headquarters to local store managers is decentralization, since authority is spread to lower levels instead of held at the top.

ww.Outsourcing work: Outsourcing work means hiring an outside firm to perform tasks, which is a different matter from moving decision authority down to local store managers.
ww.Downsizing staff: Downsizing staff means cutting the number of employees, which is about workforce size and not about who holds decision-making authority.
ww.Centralization: Centralization keeps decision authority at the top, so shifting authority from headquarters to local managers is the opposite, which is decentralization.

rw: Cutting three layers of management makes the hierarchy shorter and wider with fewer levels, so decisions travel faster, which is a flatter structure.

ww.A taller structure: A taller structure has more management layers, but she removed three layers, so the chain is shorter, not taller.
ww.A divisional structure: A divisional structure groups the firm by product or region, and cutting management layers does not change how units are grouped, only how many levels exist.
ww.A matrix structure: A matrix structure has employees reporting to two managers, which has nothing to do with removing layers to speed up decisions.

rw: Reporting to both a functional manager and a project manager is the defining feature of a matrix structure, which blends functional and project lines.

ww.A tall structure: A tall structure has many management layers and one boss per employee, while the example features dual reporting lines, which is matrix.
ww.A flat structure: A flat structure has few layers with single reporting lines, and the example's dual reporting to two managers does not fit it.
ww.A sole proprietorship: A sole proprietorship is a form of business ownership by one person, not an organizational structure for reporting lines inside a larger firm.

rw: Controlling compares actual results with goals, such as sales, to find deviations and their causes, so it is the function most directly needed to explain falling sales.

ww.Staffing: Staffing means recruiting and placing people, but sales falling each quarter calls for comparing results to goals and finding the cause, which is controlling.
ww.Advertising: Advertising is a marketing activity that might raise sales, but it is not a management function and does not diagnose why sales have been falling.
ww.Organizing: Organizing arranges people and resources, and it does not by itself analyze why performance is falling, which is the job of controlling.

rw: Praising a team publicly and giving a bonus for beating a goal motivates people, and motivating employees is the core of the leading function.

ww.Organizing tasks: Organizing tasks means arranging people and resources, whereas praising a team and giving a bonus is motivating them, which belongs to leading.
ww.Planning the goals: Planning the goals sets targets in advance, and she has already got a goal; here she is rewarding the team for beating it, which is motivation.
ww.Controlling results: Controlling results compares performance with goals to correct problems, but praise and a bonus are rewards that motivate people, which is leading.

rw: Doing everything herself so it is done right is failing to delegate, which overloads the manager, wastes the team's skills and prevents staff development.

ww.Over-delegating work: Over-delegating means handing off too much work, but saying she will do it herself shows the opposite problem, which is not delegating enough.
ww.Planning too far ahead: Planning too far ahead has nothing to do with her statement, which concerns who does the work now, not how far into the future she plans.
ww.Too much team praise: Too much team praise is not at issue, since her statement is about doing the work herself and not about how often she praises staff.

rw: Making sure every employee knows the plan and how their job helps is communicating goals, which aligns staff effort with the firm's direction.

ww.Letting workers choose: Letting workers choose does not ensure they understand the plan or how their job fits it, so it does not describe sharing the plan with employees.
ww.Locking away the plan: Locking away the plan prevents employees from knowing it, which is the opposite of what the owner wants to achieve.
ww.Hiding the plan away: Hiding the plan keeps staff in the dark, which contradicts the owner's aim that every employee know the plan and their role in it.

rw: A directive style with clear instructions fits a new, inexperienced team under a tight deadline, because they need guidance and structure to finish on time.

ww.A style that avoids setting deadlines: A style that avoids setting deadlines does not suit a tight deadline, because an inexperienced team would lack the structure and urgency it needs.
ww.A style with no direction at all given: A style with no direction would leave a new, inexperienced team without guidance, which is a poor match when time is short.
ww.A laissez-faire style leaving choices to: A laissez-faire style leaves choices to staff, which is risky for an inexperienced team that needs guidance, especially when the deadline is tight.

rw: Experienced engineers who have solved similar problems for years work best when leaders delegate and give them freedom to choose methods, which makes use of their skill.

ww.Ignoring them and their progress entirel: Ignoring the engineers and their progress is neglect and not a leadership approach, and it would waste the skills they have built up.
ww.Telling them exactly how to do each step: Telling experienced engineers exactly how to do each step is micromanagement, which wastes their expertise and tends to frustrate skilled people.
ww.Checking their work every hour of the da: Checking their work every hour is also micromanagement, which undermines the trust that skilled and experienced staff need in order to work well.

rw: Asking the team to vote on which schedule to adopt gives them a say in the decision, which is the democratic leadership style.

ww.Laissez-faire: Laissez-faire leaders leave decisions entirely to the team without guiding the process, whereas this leader puts the options to a vote, which is democratic.
ww.Autocratic: An autocratic leader makes decisions alone without input, but this leader invites the team to vote, so it is not autocratic.
ww.Transactional: A transactional leader focuses on rewards and corrections for performance, and putting the schedule choice to a team vote is a participative act.

rw: Setting a clear target, giving a bonus for meeting it and correcting those who miss is the transactional style, based on rewards and corrections.

ww.Transformational: Transformational leaders inspire followers with a vision, but this leader uses targets, bonuses and corrections, which are exchange-based features.
ww.Laissez-faire: A laissez-faire leader gives little direction, but this leader sets a clear target and rewards or corrects performance, which is the opposite.
ww.Servant-style: Servant-style leaders put the needs of their team first and remove obstacles, but this leader works through targets, bonuses and corrections instead.

rw: Servant leadership puts the team's needs first and removes obstacles in their way, so the leader acts to support the people being led.

ww.Autocratic leadership: An autocratic leader makes decisions alone and controls the team, which is unlike a leader who removes obstacles and puts team needs first.
ww.Laissez-faire style: A laissez-faire leader stays hands-off, whereas this leader actively works to help the team by removing obstacles, which is service and not absence.
ww.Transactional style: A transactional leader uses rewards and corrections for performance, and does not center on putting the team's needs first.

rw: Inspiring followers with a bold vision and encouraging them to exceed expectations is transformational leadership, which raises motivation and commitment beyond routine goals.

ww.Laissez-faire: A laissez-faire leader gives little guidance and does not inspire with a bold vision, so it does not fit the example.
ww.Autocratic style: An autocratic leader gives orders and keeps control, but this leader inspires and encourages followers, which is the opposite of that approach.
ww.Transactional: A transactional leader exchanges rewards for performance and focuses on meeting set targets, and does not inspire people to exceed expectations through vision.

rw: Situational leadership means adapting one's style to the team's skill level and the circumstances, which matches a leader who changes her approach as needs change.

ww.Transactional leadership: Transactional leadership relies on rewards and corrections and does not adapt style to the team's skill and situation, which the question describes.
ww.Laissez-faire leadership: Laissez-faire leadership is a fixed hands-off style, so it does not describe adjusting one's approach to fit the team and the situation.
ww.Autocratic leadership: Autocratic leadership is a fixed style of making decisions alone, so it does not describe a leader who changes style as conditions change.

rw: Listening and acknowledging their feelings shows empathy because the leader understands and recognizes what the person is going through before moving on.

ww.Tell them to leave their problems at hom: Telling an upset member to leave problems at home dismisses their feelings, so it lacks empathy and may damage trust.
ww.Report them for being unprofessional: Reporting them for being unprofessional punishes a person for opening up and shows no concern for them, which is the opposite of empathy.
ww.Change the subject to the deadline: Changing the subject to the deadline ignores the person's distress and shows no understanding of their feelings, so it fails to show empathy.

rw: Admitting a mistake and explaining how it will be fixed builds trust and credibility, as the team sees honesty and accountability in their leader.

ww.A reason to ignore rules: Admitting a mistake does not give a reason to ignore rules; it models accountability, and the plan to fix it supports the standards.
ww.Fear among the team: Admitting a mistake and explaining the fix does not create fear, because it shows honesty and a safe culture where people can admit errors too.
ww.Doubt about the leader: Owning the error and explaining the fix shows competence and honesty, so it reduces doubt about the leader rather than creating it.
